facts.text: The Magic Flute premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before Mozart’s death.
facts.evidence: The work premiered on 30 September 1791 at Schikaneder's theatre, the Freihaus-Theater auf der Wieden in Vienna, just two months before Mozart's death.

facts.text: At the premiere Mozart conducted, the librettist Schikaneder played Papageno himself, and the Queen of the Night was sung by Mozart’s sister-in-law, Josepha Hofer.
facts.evidence: Mozart conducted the orchestra and Schikaneder himself played Papageno, while the role of the Queen of the Night was sung by Mozart's sister-in-law Josepha Hofer.

facts.text: Mozart to his wife on 7 October 1791: “I have this moment returned from the opera, which was as full as ever … what always gives me the most pleasure is the silent approval!”
evidence: I have this moment returned from the opera, which was as full as ever
But what always gives me the most pleasure is the silent approval!

facts.text: Mozart went to hear his new opera almost every night, taking along friends and relatives.
facts.evidence: He went to hear his opera almost every night

facts.text: The opera reached its 100th performance in November 1792, but Mozart didn’t live to see it: he died on 5 December 1791.
facts.evidence: The opera celebrated its 100th performance in November 1792, though Mozart did not have the pleasure of witnessing this milestone, as he had died on 5 December 1791.

facts.text: The overture was written after the rest of the opera. Its three solemn brass chords nod to Freemasonry, where the number three is highly significant.
evidence: The overture, composed after the other parts of the opera were complete, begins with a solemn three-chord sequence from the brass
The number three is highly significant in Freemasonry

facts.text: Both Mozart and Schikaneder were Freemasons, and the opera is noted for its Masonic elements.
evidence: The Magic Flute is noted for its prominent Masonic elements

facts.text: Papageno’s whistle is based on a motif borrowed from a concerto by Antonio Salieri.
facts.evidence: Papageno's whistle is based on a motif borrowed from Salieri's Concerto for Clavicembalo in B♭ major.

facts.text: The Papageno–Papagena duet, with its bird-like syllables, resembles a comic cavatina in Salieri’s Prima la musica e poi le parole.
facts.evidence: the Papageno–Papagena duet is similar to the Cucuzze cavatina in Salieri's Prima la musica e poi le parole

facts.text: Mozart called for a “stromento d’acciaio” (instrument of steel) to play Papageno’s magic bells.
facts.evidence: Mozart also called for a stromento d'acciaio (instrument of steel) to perform Papageno's magic bells.

facts.text: The Armed Men’s chorale is set to a Baroque chorale prelude, inspired by Martin Luther’s hymn “Ach Gott, vom Himmel sieh darein”.
facts.evidence: sung to a Baroque chorale prelude, inspired by Martin Luther's hymn "Ach Gott, vom Himmel sieh darein"

facts.text: Pauline Kael called it “a peerlessly silly masterpiece: sublimely lucid music arising out of a parodistic fairy tale.”
facts.evidence: It's a peerlessly silly masterpiece: sublimely lucid music arising out of a parodistic fairy tale

facts.text: Some see the Queen of the Night as a portrait of Empress Maria Theresa, who banned Freemasonry from Austria.
facts.evidence: by others to represent Roman Catholic Empress Maria Theresa, who banned Freemasonry from Austria

facts.text: Early productions were often of highly altered, sometimes even mutilated, versions of the opera.
